newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Food situation in North Korea critical by April.
newsitem.headline: Food situation in North Korea critical by April.

text.p: North Korea, reeling from poor harvests after major floods, will need foreign food supplies by April if a serious crisis and starvation is to be averted, U.N. and aid officials said on Thursday.
But some Western donors are wary of helping the reclusive communist state and the issue remains politicised, they added.
Government rations through North Korea's public distribution system provide some 100 grams of food a day to people in flood- affected areas. Stocks are expected to run out in April or May.
A mission by several U.N. agencies, accompanied by donor representatives, is likely not to leave before March, according to U.N. sources. The team will prepare an overall U.N. appeal.

The U.N. World Food Programme appealed on Wednesday for $41.5 million to stave off "a real possibility of famine". The Rome-based agency, seeking 100,000 tonnes of food, said people were receiving a quarter of their minimum daily food needs.

"Our assessment is the same as the United Nations. The situation is bad. Starvation is possible," Simon Missiri of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) told Reuters.
"When this internal stock goes, there will be a major problem. Our assessment is that in the absence of a massive injection of food, April will mean a very serious crisis."

Missiri, deputy director of the Asia-Pacific department at the Geneva-based Federation, said: "It is not the African drought of 1995 where people died like flies. But it is very, very difficult. People are surviving on the public distribution system where rations are an average of 100 grams a day."
"We can't link food aid with any political fluctation. It is not possible. It is a matter of principle to keep telling donors that aid is required regardless of political dynamics," he said.
"Now assistance is required in every part of the population -- the capital as well as the flood-affected rural areas. It is important to have support."
Heavy floods in 1995 and 1996 have left half a million people homeless and destroyed two million tonnes of grain.
The Federation, which has been operating in North Korea since 1995, distributes food to some 139,000 people in flood-affected areas who depend entirely on these supplies.
They are the most vulnerable: large families, those headed by single mothers and people who have lost their homes. They receive a ration of 400 grams a day, according to Missiri.
"But the North Korean Red Cross reports that even among our beneficiairies there are signs of malnutrition, among children and also adults. It is very dangerous," he said.
The IFRC has raised only 16 percent of a 13.5 million Swiss franc ($10 million) appeal last November for North Korea.
It may have to slash its rations if funds do not arrive in the next weeks to purchase the 1,600 tonnes of food a month required for the 139,000 victims, according to Missiri.
"In two to three weeks time if we don't have further major contributions we have to take decisions to bring down rations.
"It is one of the most politicised aid operations. It always depends on the mood or situation of the moment," Missiri said.
With donations from national member societes including South Korean Red Cross, the IFRC kept up a steady food supply last year. But it could not manage to build any stocks or reserves.
"Each month we are in agony whether we have enough money to order food," Missiri said.
Patrick McCormick of UNICEF said: "UNICEF confirms WFP's view of the situation. This is a critical period especially concerning the state of children as rations are going down.
"There is an emergency situation. They have had nearly three years of disastrous harvests after severe weather conditions," added McCormick, who worked last year in North Korea.
UNICEF is feeding 100,000 children under age five in the flood-affected areas and has immunised nearly one million children against diseases including measles.
